prompt: You want to transpose every oscillator down one octave. Which rule works across the keyboard?

options.explanation: Correct. An octave is a ratio of two; moving down reverses the doubling.

options.text: Subtract the same number of hertz from every note
options.explanation: A fixed hertz subtraction is a different musical interval at different starting pitches.
That transposes upwards by an octave.
That gives a different interval, rather than one octave.

workedExample: Compare the frequency ratios, rather than differences. Halving a low note and halving a high note each moves down the same one-octave interval.

prompt: Which of these are correct uses of logarithms and exponentials for pitch? Select all that apply.

options.text: Transposing every note up an octave multiplies every frequency by 2
options.explanation: Correct. Adding 12 to every note number adds 1 to the exponent in the note-to-frequency formula, and adding 1 to a power of 2 doubles it.

options.text: There are exactly 4 octaves between 100 Hz and 1600 Hz
options.explanation: Correct. 1600/100 = 16 = 2⁴, so it takes four doublings: 100 → 200 → 400 → 800 → 1600.

options.text: Halfway in pitch between 220 Hz and 880 Hz is 550 Hz
options.explanation: 550 Hz is the arithmetic mean (add and halve). Halfway in pitch is the geometric mean, the square root of 220 × 880, which is 440 Hz, one octave from each.

options.text: Adding a semitone offset in note space should apply the same frequency ratio to every note
options.explanation: Correct. Equal pitch steps are equal frequency ratios; addition in note space becomes multiplication in hertz.

workedExample: An octave transpose doubles every frequency. Four successive doublings take 100 Hz to 1600 Hz. The midpoint in pitch between 220 and 880 Hz is 440 Hz because it is one octave from each, whereas 550 Hz splits the hertz difference unequally in pitch. Equal semitone offsets use the same ratio wherever they begin.
